title: Can AI create an "Explain the mistake" GCSE Maths paper?
author: Craig Barton
summary: Craig Barton asks whether ChatGPT's o1 model can turn a real GCSE maths paper into an Explain the Mistake revision resource, answering some questions correctly and others with plausible student errors. He insists pedagogically that some answers must be right, since students then cannot tell which to trust and must think hard about every one. He walks through the model's output, praising realistic errors such as a wrong denominator and a careless final-step slip, while flagging failures on image-based questions and a confident nonsense answer. He concludes the output must always be checked, and offers two classroom uses: marking a printed paper in a 4-2 independent-then-pair rhythm, or projecting answers for fast mini-whiteboard judgements.
points: Explain the Mistake tasks work best when some answers are correct, which raises the cognitive challenge and surfaces misconceptions.
ChatGPT generated believable errors, including wrong denominators and last-step slips that mirror real student behaviour.
The model struggled with images such as pictograms and coordinates, and sometimes produced confident nonsense, so teacher checking is essential.
Two classroom uses are suggested: annotated paper marking with a 4-2 approach, or slide-by-slide judgements on mini-whiteboards.
Barton frames the test of AI as whether it saves teachers time or helps them do the job better.
quotes: I am primarily interested in how AI can help teachers save time or do their jobs better (or, ideally, both). Long-time readers may remember how we have examined AI’s ability to anticipate student misconceptions, write multiple-choice questions, plan a lesson, and suggest a purpose for an upcoming topic.

Pedagogically, the answer some questions correctly part is important. I am not a fan of explain the mistake activities where each answer is wrong. The cognitive challenge and the possibility of identifying student misconceptions ramp up considerably when students do not know whether an answer is correct or not.

I like this decision. Students will be on their toes looking for errors, and so long as they do not know in advance which answers are correct and which are wrong, they will have to think just as hard about the correct answers as the wrong ones.

While this is interesting, I am unsure if it is worth sharing with our students. We know it is good practice to articulate our thinking when solving problems in front of students so our decision-making does not remain hidden, but this feels a little different.
It is becoming a cliche, but it bears repeating: Always check the output of these models carefully. While I am confident ChatGPT would get the top grade on this paper, it would not score 100%.

First, we could write ChatGPT’s working out and answers on a copy of the exam paper. We give each student a copy and ask them to mark the paper and make any necessary corrections. My 4-2 approach would work well here: giving students 4 minutes to work independently, and then 2 minutes to compare answers, and then repeat.
